content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
Summary

The paper presents a CLIP-based framework for "word-to-image" retrieval, specifically designed for high-resolution images and small objects in them. It proposes the "Complete Cover" (CC) patchification scheme to cover the image, and uses a feature fusion model to produce a single feature representation from the patches. The model is trained with a query proxy loss, and is shown to outperform raw CLIP, SLIP and RegionCLIP on LVIS, CoCo, Unity and CLEVR-DS datasets.

Strenghts

Reviewers all agree that the demonstrated inability of CLIP to retrieve visually small (and thus likely unannotated) elements of an image is an important problem, that deserves to be studied; the paper adds new experiments to that body of work (e.g. Figure 8). The proposed method is simple and intuitive and the CLEVR-DS dataset mark good steps in that direction.

Weaknesses

Reviewers agree that the paper discusses interesting questions, but find the results not convincing, only a minor improvement (or an obvious approach), and ask for ablations as well as comparisons with related work. The main issues are:

- The paper's writing and figures need improvement. Many figures do not have descriptive captions, the CC algorithm could be better explained with a figure, and important concepts such as "effective scale sensitivity" are not explained well.
- The feature fusion method is a central part of the paper, yet the authors do not provide good ablations. Table 4 shows that without CC an MLP can fuse as well as a Transformer (15.9%) - so what is the performance of MLP fusion with CC? Maybe a Transformer is not needed? Authors do not answer this question (and similar questions) in their response.
- Comparisons to previously published closely related methods such as MDETR and X-DETR are missing
- The number of objects in the image is an important factor in overall performance given the max operation in the fusion loss. This needs to be ablated in order to understand how well the model can deal with multiple objects
- The effectiveness of the proposed approach is not well justified. DetailCLIP does not perform better than CLIP with CC@10 (Table 2). The presented method is more efficient, but there is little discussion (and no ablation) of that point in the paper, although the paper claims "efficiency" as a goal of the work.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: Reviewers would consider a higher score for a paper that shows clearer differences between methods, and puts the focus slightly differently (e.g. squarely on efficiency), with more ablations. Reviewers asked substantial questions, and consistently did not increase their scores after author rebuttal. Reviewers request e.g. a deeper analysis of the fusion model (which they consider a potentially novel contribution), but authors do not provide additional insights in their rebuttal. The answer "We did use different/simpler models such as FC/MLP to fuse the features. Please have a look at section 5.3.2 and Table 4. Their performances are not as good as the tiny transformer." is insufficient, since in Table 4 the Transformer performs as well as an MLP, and the CC algorithm seems to make the difference.

content.title: We sincerely thank the Reviewer for pointing out mistakes and flows in our work. We will fix them in the next revision. We also provide some explainations for the questions.
content.comment:
* R4.1  It is hard to get the mechanism of the complete cover and figure 2 is not intuitive.
    * Figure 2 is a visualization of the Complete Cover algorithm. The small square, triangle, circle, and diamond are objects, and large squares are their covers. Also, the small square in blue ($50 \times 50$), the small triangle in yellow ($39 \times 39$), and the small circle in yellow ($2 \times 2$) are the minimum effective object for their corresponding covers with effective scale sensitivity $c=10$. The large circle and diamond are effective objects for their corresponding covers, but not the minimum effective objects. Besides, the algorithm works like a sliding window with specific kernel size and stride depending on the effective scale sensitivity and the size of the image. Detail can be seen in Appendix A.1 and Table 5. **Maybe you could give us more information on which part of the mechanism of complete cover you don't get?**
    * We will add the denotation of figure 3 in the next revision.
    * We did not choose the tiny transformer in the beginning. We did some experiments (Please have a look at section 5.3.2 and Table 4) and select the transformer in the end. 

* R4.2 The novelty of the proposed method is limited.
    * It is obtained mainly by taking maximum value along a specific dimension, but the loss we designed uses the text feature as a proxy so that the fused feature will also depend on the text feature.

* R4.3 why the authors claimed that traditional text-image retrieval datasets are not suitable for word-image retrieval
    * The word-image retrieval task needs to rank **all** relevant images on the top (or as much as possible). For example, if we have 1000 images containing "tree" in the dataset, to have a recall@1 of 100%, we need to return these 1000 images on the top. Under this task, the traditional caption-image retrieval datasets, especially the test sets suffer from the "not fully annotated" issue. From the perspective of evaluating retrieval tasks, a partially annotated dataset will lead to misinterpretation of the result. e.g., the better a model performs at top-ranking unlabeled images, the worse the retrieval score. From the perspective of evaluating "detail" retrieval tasks, the situation deteriorates. e.g., if a large and a small object of the same category are present in the same image, while one of the objects is unlabeled, despite the successful recall of the image in retrieval, we cannot tell whether it is due to the recall of the large object or the recall of the small object. Therefore rendering the evaluation of "detail" retrieval irrelevant. We visualized retrieval results of some real-world datasets, and both cases exist. 
    * A practical application in the industrial field for the word-image retrieval task is to find all the relevant images from a large image database to make a small dataset for a customized scenario by using a query. This task is as much important as the word-image retrieval task.

* R4.4 More methods should be included
  * Thank you for the suggestion. Yes, it is possible to bring more vision-language models to do the task. We will add more models such as Flamingo and GPV in the next revision.

* R4.5 the number of patches is quadratic of the size of the image
  * Yes, this is a problem theoretically. However, in practice, we can balance the Effective Scale Sensitivity and the number of patches by dropping all patches from the last few levels (see Table 11 in A.3.2). Since the difference in Minimum Effective Range between the last few levels are very small (see Table 5 in A.1).

* R4.6  More analysis should be provided to show the efficiency of training and  Generalization of the Fusion Module is doubtful.
    * Thank you for the advice. We will add more analysis on training efficiency and computational resource in the next revision. We are going to propose an open-vocab retrieval task for DetailCLIP in the future.

* R4.7 why using CLIP-ViT-B/16 and CLIP-ViT-B/14 compare with your method DetailCLIP
    * We did use ViT-B/32 (openai version CLIP) for DetailCLIP in the main experiments. 
    * For DetailCLIP in Table 3, first block, the DetailCLIP is trained with ViT-B/16 CLIP as well. We use ViT-B/16 for fair comparison (open-sourced SLIP use ViT-B/16 trained on YFCC-15M, they also released a CLIP use ViT-B/16 trained on YFCC-15M, that's what we used in the first block). 
    * For DetailCLIP in Table 3, second block, we use ViT-B/14 CLIP (openai version) to train the DetailCLIP to investigate the upper bound of the capability of CLIP and DetailCLIP. 
    * We list the performance of other models in the third block.

content.title: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the suggestions.
content.comment:
* R3.1 The definition of "Effective Scale Sensitivity" is not clear.
    * From Table 1, we know CLIP performance monotonically decreases as the object size decreases (equivalent to $r_{max}$ decreases). That means as the size of objects being smaller, they are harder to be retrieved by the CLIP model, thus harming the recall. Since we use recall@1/3/5 (which is defined in section 4.3) as metric, the result is irrelevant with accuracy and specific object (we measure the overall performance for the entire dataset at given $r_{max}$).

* R3.2 why not use a different/simpler fusion model
    * We did use different/simpler models such as FC/MLP to fuse the features. Please have a look at section 5.3.2 and Table 4. Their performances are not as good as the tiny transformer.

* R3.3 comparison to the previously published methods, such as MDETR and X-DETR
  * Thank you for the suggestion. We will add more models such as MDETR and XDETR in the next revision.

* R3.4 an ablation regarding the number of object details the model can fuse in a single feature would be interesting to see.
  * Thank you for the comment. Yes, we agree that's an interesting experiment, and CLEVR-DS can generate the relevant dataset (control the number of objects in the image) easily. We will design this ablation study in the next revision to see how much detail information can be compressed into a 512-dim feature.

* R3.5&3.6 an experiment measuring the ability to capture local objects vs. the ability to capture the global information of the image (as in vanilla CLIP) would be useful
    * Figure 2 is a visualization of the Complete Cover algorithm. The small square, triangle, circle, and diamond are objects, and large squares are their covers. Also, the small square in blue ($50 \times 50$), the small triangle in yellow ($39 \times 39$), and the small circle in yellow ($2 \times 2$) are the minimum effective object for their corresponding covers with effective scale sensitivity $c=10$. The large circle and diamond are effective objects for their corresponding covers, but not the minimum effective objects. Besides, the algorithm works like a sliding window with specific kernel size and stride depending on the effective scale sensitivity and the size of the image. Detail can be seen in Appendix A.1 and Table 5.

* R3.7 typos
    * We will fix them in the next revision.

content.title: We sincerely thank the Reviewer for the insightful comments. We address our points and further explaination below.
content.comment:
* R2.1 does not include other models for comparison.

    * It is not practical to use the same amount of data to retrain the models you mentioned above. We will include the results for models such as XDETR, GLIP, GLIPv2, mDETR, etc. using pre-trained weights in the next revision.


* R2.2 does not include other models for comparison.

  * Thank you for the suggestion. We will add a section for other tasks such as classification, detection, etc. in the next revision.


* R2.3 why "use a word to retrieve all related images in a database" is necessary compared to retrieving top-k samples? The proposed metric is specifically tailored for the task of retrieving "all" relevant images, which is aligned with the proposed model's strength.
    * A practical application in the industrial field is to find all the relevant images from a large image database to make a small dataset for a customized scenario by using a query. There is only **one ground-truth image for a caption query** in the traditional text2image retrieval task, so it is appropriate to use the recall@k as the metric. In our benchmark, we don't have the caption for each image and what we have is the name of the class. Therefore, we use the name of the class with predefined prompt templates to generate a weak caption (not descriptive as the customized caption) as the query. That results **more than one ground-truth images for a weak caption query as long as the image contains the object that belongs to that class**. The traditional metric is not appropriate to be used here, and the proposed metric is to solve this problem. We will include an experiment to show which k method provides its benefit in the next revision.

* R2.4 Captions of some figures are not descriptive (e.g. Figures 1, 3, 4).
    * Thank you for the suggestion. We will improve the caption for Figures 1, 3, 4 in the next revision.

content.title: We sincerely thank the reviewer for all the comments. We address our points and further explanation below.
content.comment:
* R1.1 DetailCLIP does not perform significantly better than CLIP with CC@10

    * It is reasonable that some results of CC@10 perform better than some results of DetailCLIP since the feature of DetailCLIP should be compared with vanilla CLIP feature, which are both single features with the same dimension (e.g. 512) for an image. As you can see, the result of DetailCLIP is significantly better than vanilla CLIP. CC@10 has 166 features for an image, and each of them is a 512-dimension feature. If one of the 166 features has a top rank, the image will be retrieved, which reduces the difficulty of the retrieval task. Therefore, it is not appropriate to use the result of CC@10 **features** to compare the result of the DetailCLIP **feature**. 

    * There are two advantages of the DetailCLIP feature we want to emphasize. Firstly, detailed information from CC@10 features is compressed into one feature, which makes us achieve more than 100 times reduction for the number of patches with no significant performance loss. Secondly, because of the loss we used, the DetailCLIP feature and vanilla CLIP feature are in the same feature space, which means the feature from DetailCLIP can perform the downstream task proposed by CLIP as well with an emphasis on object details.

* R1.2 The presentation of the paper can be improved.
    * Thanks for the advice, and we will work on improving the presentation of the paper in the next revision.

* R1.3 The efficiency of the proposed approach compared with CLIP is not discussed.
    * We did mention the efficiency of the proposed approach compared with CLIP implicitly in Appendix 3.1 in terms of the number of patch reductions (which is closely related to the efficiency of the DetailCLIP and vanilla CLIP), and we will explicitly compare the efficiency (e.g. time comparison) of the proposed approach with CLIP in the next revision.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes introduce an efficient framework that can produce a single feature representation for a high-resolution image that injects image details and shares the same semantic space as the original CLIP. The authors train a feature fusing model on CLIP features extracted from a carefully designed image patch method (Complete Cover) that can cover objects of any scale, weakly supervised by image-agnostic class prompted queries. The framework is validated by retrieving images from class prompted queries on the existing real-world and synthetic datasets. The authors also construct the synthetic CLVER-DS dataset, which is fully annotated and has a controllable object scale, to validate the proposed approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. How to capture the detailed information in images by CLIP model is a challenging and important problem to investigate.
2. The proposed CLEVR-DS dataset will benefit future research on this direction.

Weaknesses:
1. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is not well justified. According to Table 2, DetailCLIP does not perform significantly better than CLIP with CC@10. The improvement is marginal and sometimes DetailCLIP is even worse than CLIP with CC@10. Table 3 also shows that DetailCLIP performs worse on LVIS dataset. So the current experiments does not show the effectiveness of the proposed DetailCLIP.
2. The presentation of the paper can be improved.
3. The efficiency of the proposed approach compared with CLIP is not discussed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear but the writing and presentation can be improved. The proposed approach is somewhat novel but not super exciting.
content.summary_of_the_review: The major problem of the paper is that the effectiveness of the proposed method is not well justified by the experiments (see 1 in the weaknesses section). Current experiments are limited and cannot support the author's claims.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents DetailCLIP, a CLIP-like framework for text-to-image retrieval specifically designed for high-resolution images. It proposes a patch selection scheme (Complete Cover) to cover the image efficiently, and uses a feature fusion model to produce a single feature representation for high-resolution images. The model is trained with a query proxy loss (equation 7), and is shown to outperform CLIP, SLIP and RegionCLIP on LVIS, CoCo, Unity and CLEVR-DS datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**: 

- The paper presents an approach to enhance text-to-image retrieval capability of CLIP-like models on high-resolution images. Experiments demonstrate improved performance on this task compared to the baselines. 

**Weaknesses**:

- There are other papers such as XDETR, GLIP, GLIPv2, mDETR, etc. that add retrieval and detection capabilities to the CLIP model. The authors mention some of these papers in the introduction and say "they all require enormous training data and computational resources to complete". However, they do not provide any fair comparison with these methods using similar amount of data and computational resources. Specifically, X-DETR performs multi-modal instance search, which is quite similar to the retrieval task discussed in the paper. 
  
- The paper merely focuses on the text-to-image retrieval task for high-resolution images. It is unclear whether the proposed model is applicable to any other tasks such as classification, detection, etc. Does the proposed model maintain/improve zero-shot classification performance of the CLIP model?

- The authors mention that "in many practical scenarios, we need to use a word to retrieve all related images in a database" in the introduction, and define the task and the metric accordingly. However, they do not provide more details on why this is necessary compared to retrieving top-k samples. 

- The proposed metric is specifically tailored for the task of retrieving "all" relevant images, which is aligned with the proposed model's strength. The authors can compare top-k recall of their method with baselines and show at which k their method provides its benefit.

- Captions of some figures are not descriptive (e.g. Figure 1, 3, 4).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
$+$ The proposed approach is simple and intuitive and provides improvements in text-to-image retrieval for high-resolution images.  
$-$ The problem scope is limited to text-to-image retrieval and it is unclear if the proposed model retains properties of the CLIP model or provides any additional properties.  
$-$ Fair comparison with prior work (e.g. X-DETR) is not provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed approach improves text-to-image retrieval capability of the CLIP model for high-resolution images; however, the problem scope and the performance evaluation are limited, and comparison with prior work is not conclusive.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper aims to learn an image representation model that is able to represent high resolution images while capturing both the global context and the local details (e.g. different objects in the image) such that the representation lies in CLIP's original feature space. To illustrate, such a representation can allow querying an images using a text query that refers to specific object that are presented in the image, but are not the "main" global text annotation of the image (e.g. : return all image containing a red hat). Specifically, the proposed method tries to fuse CLIP features extracted from different patches in the image where the patches correspond to the objects in the image. 

To this end, the paper presents the "Complete Cover" method which extracts patches from the image such that the set of extracted patches contains all objects present and a fusion model which fuses the features from the different extracted patches. The fusion model is chosen to be a shallow transformer and is trained by minimising the different between 1. similarity of text embedding corresponding to the object class and the patch feature of the object and 2. the similarity of the text embedding corresponding to the object class and the fused feature. 

The paper presents experiments comparing the proposed method with the baseline of using a single CLIP feature for the image and the baseline of using CLIP features extracted from each patch.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The paper addresses an important limitation of "CLIP-like" models to capture local detail information in image as opposed to learning the global information in an image. 

Weaknesses:
I have a few concerns regarding the following points:
1. The definition of "Effective Scale Sensitivity" is not clear. It is defined as as the "minimum object occupying percentage in an image that CLIP-like models can retrieve" - retrieve with what accuracy? on which objects? I think this point should be better explained. 

2. The method uses a shallow transformer to fuse the features, why not use a different/simpler model? How would that affect the results? I would expect to see some discussion and an ablation study on that aspect.

3. The experiments only consider the baselines of running CLIP on the complete image and on patches extracted by the proposed Complete Cover algorithm. In my opinion, a comparison to previously published method, such as MDETR and X-DETR, should also be presented in the paper.

4. There is no discussion regarding the influence of the number of objects in the image on the fused feature and the model performance. Given that the fusion model has limited capacity, an ablation regarding the number of object details the model can fuse in a single feature would be interesting to see.

5. The loss encourages the fused feature similarity to the proxy feature to be close to the proxy feature similarity to the corresponding patch feature. In that case, the loss can be minimised by having the fused feature capture only the specific patch feature and ignoring all other patches. How is that prevented in the fused feature? an experiment measuring the ability to capture local objects vs. the ability to capture the global information of the image (as in vanilla CLIP) would be useful to clear this point. 

6. In terms of presentation - a figure visualising of the Complete Cover algorithm can improve the readability of the paper. 

7. Minor concern, typos:
page 2 - "The problem motioned above", should be "mentioned"
page 7 - "CILP-like", should be CLIP like
page 9 - "upper bond", upper bound
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: In my opinion, several limitations and aspects of the method are not thoroughly discussed or evaluated. Also, it's not clear that the method is indeed stronger than previously presented methods as only simple CLIP-based baseline are used for comparison.
content.summary_of_the_review: As written above, I have a few concerns regarding the quality and the clarity of the work as several limitations and aspects of the method are not thoroughly discussed. Also, the technical novelty of the paper is limited in my opinion and the experiments only consider simple baselines.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to solve the problem that when using CLIP for text-image retrieval, it usually has a poor performance when recognizing objects of small size in the images due to the constrains of CLIP feature size and size of input image. This paper proposes a fusion module to collapse CLIP features of multiple patches into a single one. Since patches with different sizes capture different level of details, leveraging them together helps to bake in more details into CLIP features. Besides, the authors also created a dataset called CLEVR-DS which has more object classes and more object sizes than CLEVR.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The experiment showing that CLIP performance is sensitive to the spatial fraction of objects with regard to the whole image is interesting.

Weaknesses:
1. The writing of this paper is bad. It is hard to get the mechanism of complete cover and the figure 2 is not intuitive. Figure 3 does not provide clarifications of denotations. The rationale of why using transformer as the structure of fusing model is not clear.
2. The novelty of the proposed method is limited. The proposed complete cover is basically a matching algorithm taking advantage to spatial pyramid. Collapsing different patches into one through supervised loss is also trivial as the groundtruth is obtained mainly by taking maximum value along a specific dimension.
3. I don't understand why the authors claimed that traditional text-image retrieval datasets are not suitable for word-image retrieval since those datasets are targeting for caption-image retrieval and in my perspective, caption-image retrieval is harder and more general than word-image retrieval task. 
4. The method is only compared to a few methods. More methods should be included. I wonder if it is possible to turn vision-language models like Flamingo, GPV [1], etc. into some methods that can be compared to.
5. For the proposed Complete Cover algorithm, the paper shows that the number of patches is quadratic of the size of the image. It is a large number when the Effective Scale Sensitivity we want is small. 
6. The effectiveness of the Fusion Module is achieved by only focusing on the object categories in the target dataset. This brought two problems:	
	a)       Training is necessary to fit the Fusion Module, which can be time and computational resource consuming. More analysis should be provided to show the efficiency of training.
	b)      Generalization of the Fusion Module is doubtful. It is a question whether the Fusion Module can still be used when the training dataset and test dataset do not have the same labels. 
7. In Sec. 5.2.2, why using CLIP-ViT-B/16 and CLIP-ViT-B/14 compare with your method DetailCLIP? Since in 5.2.1 you mentioned that the backbone for DetailCLIP is ViT-B/32.
[1] Gupta T, Kamath A, Kembhavi A, et al. Towards general purpose vision systems[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2104.00743, 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is not good as I explained in the previous section.

I don’t think the idea of Completer Cover is novel, since it is basically a matching algorithm taking advantage to spatial pyramid. Besides, since CLEVR already provided convenient method to generate new images, the contribution of dataset CLEVR-DS is less significant.
content.summary_of_the_review: The main contribution of this paper is providing a framework named DetailCLIP which can compress CLIP image features of multiple patches into one, with less loss of information of current dataset. This framework requires the training of Fusion Module to be efficient or the pre-trained Fusion Module has great transferability to another dataset. These two points should be shown more clearly in the paper. The other two contributions claimed by the paper, image patching scheme “Complete Cover” and the retrieval benchmark CLEVR-DS are not so significant.

content.title: Injecting Image Details into CLIP's Feature Space
content.TL;DR: We propose a framework, including a model-agnostic complete cover scheme to obtain image patches, a fusing model, the corresponding query proxy loss and a new text-image retrieval benchmark.
content.abstract: Although CLIP-like Visual Language Models provide a functional joint feature space for image and text, due to the limitation of the CILP-like model's image input size (e.g., 224), subtle details are lost in the feature representation if we input high-resolution images (e.g., 2240). In this work, we introduce an efficient framework that can produce a single feature representation for a high-resolution image that injects image details and shares the same semantic space as the original CLIP. In the framework, we train a feature fusing model based on CLIP features extracted from a carefully designed image patch method (Complete Cover) that can cover objects of any scale, weakly supervised by image-agnostic class prompted queries. We validate our framework by retrieving images from class prompted queries on the existing real-world and synthetic datasets, showing significant performance improvement on these tasks. Furthermore, to fully demonstrate our framework's detail retrieval ability, we construct a CLEVR-like synthetic dataset called CLVER-DS, which is fully annotated and has a controllable object scale.
